hn.fm: what was found and what was done

The article on this site describes a hackathon project from September 2025: Hacker News stories turned into narrated video by a language model, a speech model and an image model on one PC. The project kept growing after the article. By this autumn it had a Postgres database, a triage step that scores stories, a daily digest sent to an e-reader, a Helm chart, a build pipeline, and the beginnings of an internet radio station.
The deployed copy had been failing quietly.

Its text model route no longer answered and had no fallback, so every model call on the cluster returned an error. The image service it pointed at had been replaced by a newer one under a different name. Nothing on its status page said so.
The radio had never run on the cluster.
It worked on a laptop. The chart's radio templates had never been rendered with the switch on.
One prompt had never worked as written.
The prompt for the station's short comedy bits put its style guide in a part of the file that is sent as-is, so the model received the literal text

The old station asked a model to invent thirty minutes of programming, then ran 170 lines of code to repair what came back. The rebuild swaps the jobs. Code owns the shape of the hour; the model owns the choices inside it.
, each with two hosts, a tone and its own music: Cold Start, Main Thread, The Diff, Show and Tell, Night Shift, Garbage Collection.
for each show: four quarters, each an ordered list of slots. A slot is a segment type.

, among them a two-hander, a phone-in where callers voice points from the comment thread down a telephone line, a top-of-the-hour bulletin, the front page read as a weather forecast, a mock sponsor read, and a song of the hour.
One question for the model per block
: which story goes in which slot. Anything it returns that does not fit is replaced by rule.
: a fact sheet per story, a draft, rule checks, an editor prompt, one rewrite, and a final pass that cuts any sentence the rules still reject.
: every spoken line is transcribed by a speech recogniser and compared with its script. A line that came out wrong is spoken again.
: with no listener the station plays music from its library and leaves the models alone. Someone tuning in wakes it. Three scheduled editions a day keep the archive growing.
: each finished block is kept as one file, with a podcast feed.

The second pass: fewer things, made better

Brian's direction after hearing the station was to stop making radio around the clock and put the effort into the quality of what is made and into running the project from one place. Production was switched off the same hour. What followed:

Twelve effects are synthesised from sine waves and noise by ffmpeg, with no recordings: the pips before the bulletin, a ring and a click before a caller, static around a correspondent, a whoosh and a low hit around the announcer. Six treatments say where a voice is speaking from: the studio, a phone, a line from outside, the announcer's big voice, fine print read fast at the end of an advert. Segments name their effects in code. The model never chooses a sound.

Measuring the speech model showed every mood is a different voice (calm runs 40 to 90 per cent slower; only one host can sound happy, only two fearful) and that four speakers the station never used can be understood in English. There are now six hosts, three correspondents, an announcer and twelve caller voices.
A cold open cut from the opening lines of the pieces that follow it, with no model call. The front page as a countdown. A report from a correspondent.

A whole hour of a show is made as one programme with chapter marks, a transcript, cover art drawn by the image model, a page where the line being spoken is lit, and a video. The first, an hour of the morning show: 32 of 32 items, 21 minutes 38 seconds, made in about five minutes, speech matching its script at 0.96.
One page with a column each for reading, radio and video: what was last made, a button to make the next, and its switch. Radio production is now a setting, not a deploy.

Two findings from this pass belong with the ones below. Given a paragraph describing a host's character, the model read it out as copy; of a story about a teacher assaulted by a student it wrote that the host "counts that among the small clever things that delight her". Character sheets are now two lines about manner, and any sentence sharing four words with one is cut. And asked to stop borrowing from the worked example, the model more than once handed back the example itself; the borrowed sentence is now cut by rule and the earlier draft kept. On the same twelve stories as before: none failed (one had), all twelve passed the rules (eleven had), eleven passed the editor (ten had).

What is still not good, from reading that first episode: headlines that are a list of facts with no shape, one that made no sense, callers who introduce themselves as members of a demographic, and a two-host conversation that ran thirteen turns (now held to eight). The structure and the sound are the station's; the sentences are the local model's, and it shows.
The text model is fast and small. It answers in about a second. Four things about it shaped the design more than any plan did.
Told to "open on the hook", it wrote "The hook: seven years of updates." Labels in the input were read out too. The input now has no labels, and a rule cuts any sentence that recites.
It cannot be told to think a little.

With thinking on it produced four thousand tokens of reasoning and no answer, whatever budget was requested. Everything runs with thinking off. The writer fills in three short fields first (the hook, the facts, the ending) and then writes, which is thinking at a fixed price.
It follows an example and ignores a rule.
Each segment type has one worked example. A test holds the examples to the station's own rules, because an example that breaks a rule teaches the opposite.
It copies whatever it is shown.

Given the research brief, it read the brief back. Given the earlier items in the block for continuity, it lifted whole sentences from them into unrelated stories. It is now shown only a short fact sheet for the story in hand.
Its editor prompt is the weak part. It scores nearly everything five out of five. The rules written in code are what hold quality.
Was it better? A measured answer

The same twelve stories were written twice: once by the old prompt (the title, then three bullet points read aloud) and once by the rebuilt writers' room. Both sets went through the same rule checks and the same editor.
Mean length (the slot wants about 70 words)
Pieces with nothing for the rules to object to
Pieces where nothing usable was written

Then a stronger model read the twelve pairs as a listener, without being told which was which. It preferred the new piece in seven pairs and the old in three, with two ties. That reading is not fully blind, because a piece that opens on its own title is recognisably the old format.

The more useful result was what the reading found. Four defects in the new pipeline showed up in those twelve pairs, and each was fixed the same hour with a test: a sentence cut in the middle of a spelled-out acronym, invented callers, "10th" read as "ten th", and notes about "the source" read on air. A second read of the two weakest segment types found four more. Measuring was worth more than the score.

So the honest summary is: clearly better, not ten times better, at two and a half times the model time per piece. The gains that are closer to tenfold are structural. The station costs nothing when nobody listens. A wrong word no longer reaches the air unheard. A new segment type is one entry in one file.

Everything so far was done by one model, Claude Fable 5.2, working in a terminal session with access to the repositories and read access to the cluster. The comparison Brian asked for, the same tasks handed to a local model through Hermes, has not been run yet. The radio work is a preview of what it will show: the local model is a capable writer inside a tight structure and an unreliable judge of its own work.

hn.fm story videos: a narrated story is now one HyperFrames composition, and the Hermes agent directs it. For each scene the agent returns a small card (a figure, a comparison, bars, a list, a phrase and so on), code checks the card against the narration and builds the scene. The agent works from a profile with no tools and its own key.
A check of every model on the desk. Eight of ten answer. No model that can read pictures is running, which is the one real gap; the video-clip model is stopped on purpose.
